strengths: Clear Datasets/Benchmarks contribution: Affogato is by a wide margin the largest and most diverse 3D affordance grounding dataset (150K objects from Objaverse, >750K open-vocabulary text-heatmap pairs), and the paper is, to the authors' credit, the first to unify 3D and 2D affordance grounding data from a single source.

The Affogato-Engine pipeline (Gemma3 query generation -> Molmo pointing -> SAM masks -> multi-view 2D-to-3D voting aggregation) is well motivated, clearly documented, and reproducible in principle; implementation details (models, views, GPU budget) are provided in the appendix.

The evaluation split construction is thoughtful: human-verified quality ratings on 5K pairs, exclusion from training, and manual refinement of 'not good' annotations, which mitigates some concerns about fully automated annotation pipelines.

Experiments are reasonably broad: cross-dataset evaluation with LASO, within-dataset open-vocabulary cross-domain splits on non-overlapping categories, zero-shot and fine-tuned evaluation on AGD20K for 2D, plus an Affogato-Partial variant simulating partial observability. The claimed generalization benefits of training on Affogato are supported.

The paper honestly analyzes failure modes of its own pipeline (VLM category confusion, SAM edge bias, occlusion) and limitations (no backgrounds, contact-point-only supervision), and discusses metric caveats such as MAE's sensitivity to annotation scale.
Reproducibility support is good: dataset is shared publicly, baselines are publicly available, and architecture/training details are sufficiently complete.
weaknesses: The benchmark advantage over baselines is confounded by backbone strength: Espresso-3D uses a pretrained PartField encoder with frozen encoders while OpenAD and PointRefer use older/weaker backbones, so gains on the Affogato benchmark conflate dataset quality with architecture. A stronger 3D AffordanceLLM-style baseline (or re-implementations with matched backbones) is missing.

Annotation quality is only partially established: 72.3% 'good' with 15.4% 'not good' implies substantial label noise in the training portion (only the test split is refined), and the paper does not quantify the effect of this noise or train-set curation on model performance. The small test split (~1K objects / 5K pairs) also limits statistical strength of the proposed benchmark.

The coverage/diversity comparison in Fig. 3d is not apples-to-apples: coverage and per-object KL-diversity are computed between Affogato annotations and LASO's annotations, which derive from a much sparser human annotation protocol; the numbers therefore do not isolate annotation quality, and no agreement-with-human-ground-truth metric on shared objects is reported in the main text (qualitative appendix only).

Several methodological choices are under-justified: five queries per object generated by a relatively small Gemma3-4B may limit query diversity/quality; the sigmoid of SAM logits as 'probabilistic heatmaps' inherits SAM's boundary bias, which the authors themselves acknowledge; and the voting aggregation details are only described qualitatively.

Absolute performance of the models on 3D tasks remains low (e.g., aIoU of 0.136 on Affogato, and cross-domain aIoU of 0.046 for Furniture->Daily-used), suggesting the open-vocabulary task is far from solved; the paper could better contextualize whether low scores reflect metric/annotation ambiguity or genuine difficulty.

External validation is limited to AGD20K for 2D; a comparison against the more recent 3D AffordanceLLM/IRAS or SeqAfford-style approaches, even qualitatively, would strengthen the claim that Affogato supersedes existing 3D datasets. As a benchmark paper, releasing reference code/leaderboard infrastructure should also be confirmed.

Minor presentation issues: duplicated reference [53]/[54]; Fig. 3d metrics are described only briefly; some claims (e.g., 'overcome the multi-view inconsistency problem' in stage 3) are stated without quantitative multi-view consistency evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: existing 3D affordance datasets derive from a single 23-class asset source (PartNet), and 2D datasets are small and closed-vocabulary. A 150K-instance, 750K-query open-vocabulary dataset is a substantial and useful contribution to the community.

The automated Affogato-Engine pipeline (Gemma3 query generation -> Molmo pointing -> SAM masks -> multi-view 2D-to-3D voting) is clearly described, scalable (~24h on 8 H100s), and reusable by others; the design choices (CoT prompting, view aggregation, background augmentation) are documented in sufficient detail to reproduce.

The paper is unusually candid about limitations: MAE metric instability, SAM's edge bias, occluded parts, lack of background context, and the need for VLM-generated data to eventually extend beyond contact points. This transparency is appreciated.

Evidence goes beyond self-evaluation on the authors' own benchmark: models pretrained on Affogato show smaller cross-dataset generalization gaps on LASO and improve state-of-the-art results on the external AGD20K benchmark, which supports the claim that the dataset provides transferable supervision rather than only self-consistent supervision.

The 2D dataset derived by projecting 3D heatmaps with verified geometric alignment is a nice bridging contribution, unifying 3D and 2D affordance grounding streams for the first time; the human-verified/refined test split partially mitigates concerns about synthetic label noise in evaluation.
weaknesses: The dataset quality rests heavily on VLM predictions, creating a circularity risk: models are trained on outputs of Gemma3/Molmo/SAM and may inherit and amplify their biases (e.g., SAM's documented edge bias is acknowledged, yet edge-biased training data remains in the training split, not just the test split). The human verification covers only 1K objects / 5K pairs (~0.7% of queries), and 15.4% of sampled annotations were rated 'not good'—extrapolated to the full 750K pairs this implies a large volume of noisy training labels with no measurement of inter-annotator agreement or annotation protocol reliability.

The claimed superiority in heatmap 'coverage' and 'diversity' over prior datasets (Tab. 3d) is measured with metrics defined by the authors (KL divergence between annotations, union-of-annotation coverage). Affogato's annotations are continuous probability heatmaps from a multi-view aggregation procedure, while prior datasets' annotations are sparse point labels; comparing these under the authors' own metric is not clearly apples-to-apples and may structurally favor the new data.

Espresso is a minimal adaptation of existing components (PartField backbone, OOAL architecture, SAM-style transformer decoder) with frozen encoders and a text-conditional decoder; this is fine as a baseline but limits the methodological contribution—the paper's scientific case rests almost entirely on the dataset, so dataset validation rigor matters a great deal, and the validation described above is not fully convincing.

All 3D data derives from synthetic Objaverse/G-Objaverse renders; there is no evaluation on real-world scanned 3D data (e.g., ARKitScenes-style or ScanNet objects), leaving open whether the learned affordances transfer beyond clean synthetic assets. The Affogato-Partial extension (appendix) only partially addresses this by simulating occlusion, not realism.

The comparison against OpenAD and PointRefer in Tables 2/3 is somewhat confounded: Espresso-3D uses a much stronger, recently pretrained 3D backbone (PartField) than the baselines, so it is unclear whether wins on the Affogato benchmark reflect dataset quality, backbone quality, or both. A backbone-controlled comparison (e.g., PointRefer/OpenAD with the PartField encoder, or Espresso with their encoders) would strengthen the dataset's evidentiary value.

Potential data contamination is not discussed: Gemma3 and Molmo have very likely seen Objaverse-related imagery/text during pretraining, which could inflate the apparent quality and diversity of generated annotations; nor is there discussion of Objaverse asset licensing/redistribution terms for a public 150K-asset release.

The 2D zero-shot comparison in Table 4a pits a supervised-trained specialist model against general-purpose VLM baselines evaluated with a fixed prompt template ('Point to the part that...'); prompt sensitivity of the zero-shot baselines is not explored, making the headline zero-shot win less meaningful than it appears. Note also duplicate references ([53] and [54] are the same MobileSAM paper), indicating loose bibliography hygiene.

strengths: Substantial dataset contribution appropriate to a Datasets/Benchmarks-type paper: Affogato is 150K 3D instances with 750K open-vocabulary query-heatmap pairs across both 3D and 2D modalities, roughly an order of magnitude beyond prior affordance datasets in scale and diversity (Table 1), and is the first effort to unify 3D and 2D affordance grounding from a single data source.

The Affogato-Engine pipeline (Gemma3 for query generation, Molmo for pointing, SAM for mask decoding, multi-view projection and voting) is a sensible, scalable, and fully documented automatic annotation recipe; the appendix provides concrete model versions, view sampling, compute, and timing, supporting reproducibility.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for a dataset paper: in-dataset and cross-dataset comparison (Table 2), open-vocabulary cross-category splits (Table 3), zero-shot 2D transfer to AGD20K against strong VLM baselines (Table 4a), and fine-tuning results showing Affogato pretraining yields SOTA on AGD20K-Full (Table 4b). The cross-dataset gap analysis is a convincing way to demonstrate that dataset diversity improves generalization.

Human verification of the test split (5K pairs, three-tier rating, refinement of 'not good' samples) with a described annotation UI and criteria adds credibility to the benchmark's evaluation quality.

Good self-awareness: the paper honestly discusses Affogato-Engine failure modes (LLM misidentification, SAM edge bias, occlusion of functional parts), the MAE metric's sensitivity to annotation scale, limitations of synthetic backgrounds, and provides Affogato-Partial as a realistic partial-observability variant.

The proposed Espresso baseline is simple, clearly specified (frozen PartField + Recap-CLIP for 3D, frozen DINOv2 + CLIP for 2D), and ablations (background augmentation, frozen encoders) support the design choices.
weaknesses: Potential circularity bias: the entire training annotation set is generated by Gemma3+Molmo+SAM, and the paper itself acknowledges systematic failure modes (SAM edge bias, LLM category confusion). Models trained on Affogato may partly learn the generator's biases rather than ground-truth human affordance, and the paper provides no quantitative human-vs-annotation agreement beyond the 72.3% 'good' / 15.4% 'not good' rating on 5K pairs (no inter-annotator agreement, no per-criterion breakdown).

The generalization claims in Table 2 require careful reading: the headline claim of 'smaller gaps' holds mainly via normalized percentage-point drops relative to in-dataset performance, while absolute LASO performance of Affogato-trained Espresso-3D (aIoU 0.067) is well below LASO-trained PointRefer (0.192). Since the two benchmarks use different annotation protocols, part of the apparent cross-dataset robustness may reflect distributional differences in annotation style rather than true semantic generalization.

The Affogato benchmark evaluation is thin: only two existing methods (OpenAD, PointRefer) are retrained; no results from stronger recent systems such as 3D AffordanceLLM/IRAS or SeqAfford, which would better establish the benchmark's difficulty and headroom.

Several presentation/consistency issues undermine polish: references [53] and [54] are duplicate citations of the FasterSAM paper while the SAM mask decoder is actually [20]/[51]; Figure A2 attributes 3D-AffordanceNet ground truth to reference [36] (which is VRB, not AffordanceNet); Table A2 reports consistently higher aIoU/AUC on Partial than Full views for all methods, which is counterintuitive and not adequately explained.

The coverage/diversity comparison (Fig. 3d) is not entirely apples-to-apples: LASO has few queries per object (870 total), so KL-divergence-based 'diversity' inherently favors a dataset with 5 queries per object; the metric definitions favor Affogato by construction.

Only one external 2D benchmark (AGD20K) is used, and all Affogato 2D data are renders of Objaverse assets; a real-image 3D or 2D evaluation (e.g., 3DOI or egocentric data) would strengthen the cross-domain claims. Objaverse asset licensing/redistribution terms and data provenance are not discussed.

Only test-split annotations are human-refined; training data (with ~15% 'not good' estimated quality) are used as-is, and the paper does not report whether filtering or reweighting noisy training annotations changes model performance.

strengths: Strong Datasets/Benchmarks contribution: Affogato-750K is an order of magnitude larger and far more diverse than prior 3D affordance datasets (Table 1), addressing a genuine bottleneck (closed-vocabulary, manually annotated data) in affordance grounding.

Fully automated annotation pipeline chaining Gemma3, Molmo, and MobileSAM with multi-view lifting and voting is well motivated and clearly described; error mitigation (CoT prompting, multi-view consensus, smallest-mask selection) is analyzed with dedicated ablations (Fig. 8, Sec. C.1).

Careful evaluation design: a 5K human-verified test split with 10 hired annotators, transparent reporting of pipeline failure modes (84.8% success rate with a failure taxonomy), a held-out category filtering experiment (Table 5) that credibly rules out overlap-driven gains, a data-scaling study (Table A3), and a cross-domain asymmetry analysis (Table A4) all strengthen the scientific case.

Espresso-3D/2D baselines are a sensible design choice for isolating the dataset's contribution from architectural confounds, and results show consistent pretraining gains for both the new models and prior methods (OpenAD, PointRefer) across 2D and 3D benchmarks, including zero-shot transfer to real robot scenes (Fig. 7).
Reproducibility support is good: model versions, compute resources, training hyperparameters, and an annotation UI are documented in the appendix; limitations and failure cases are openly discussed.
weaknesses: Annotation quality is inherited from foundation models: only 84.8% of verified pairs pass, with dominant systematic errors (wrong interaction points 34.9%, wrong queries 36.8% including object misidentification). The 750K training annotations are unverified, so systematic model biases (e.g., Molmo pointing errors, SAM edge bias) may be baked into the supervision and could be amplified by pretrained models; only qualitative (Fig. A2), not quantitative, comparison against human annotations is provided for the training data.

The human-verified test split is small (5K pairs) relative to the dataset's claimed diversity, and evaluation on the Affogato-750K benchmark (Table 3) compares only retrained versions of OpenAD/PointRefer/Espresso, so the new benchmark's discriminative power remains to be demonstrated by the community.

Validation of real-world/robotic utility is purely qualitative (Fig. 7); no quantitative zero-shot numbers on a real-image affordance benchmark are given, leaving the sim-to-real claim weakly supported.

Some experimental margins are modest (e.g., PointRefer on LASO seen degrades with pretraining; AGD20K-unseen KLD saturates by 400K pairs), and the paper does not deeply analyze when pretraining gains vanish.

Writing has redundancy (Section 3 motivation repeats the introduction nearly verbatim), and the dataset license/redistribution terms for derivative Objaverse assets are not discussed, which matters for release and reuse.

Contribution type is not explicitly declared; if treated as Algorithms/General rather than Datasets/Benchmarks, the modeling contribution (Espresso) is intentionally minimal and the case would be weaker. Judged as a Datasets/Benchmarks paper, the evidence is appropriate and convincing.

strengths: The paper addresses a real bottleneck in affordance grounding research: the lack of large-scale, open-vocabulary training data. The automated pipeline (Gemma3 for query generation, Molmo for pointing, MobileSAM for segmentation, multi-view voting for 3D lifting) is well-motivated and clearly described, and the 750K-annotation scale is far beyond prior datasets (Table 1).

Reliability is taken seriously: a 5K human-verified test split with 10 annotators, explicit reporting of pipeline failure modes (84.8% success rate, per-stage error breakdown in Fig. 4 and Appendix C), and a held-out test pool with no instance/view/query overlap.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for a dataset paper: pretraining gains are shown for multiple architectures (OpenAD, PointRefer, Espresso) on external benchmarks (LASO, AGD20K), a held-out category filtering experiment (Table 5) guards against the trivial explanation that gains come from covering held-out classes, scale ablations (Table A3) support the 'at scale' claim, and cross-domain asymmetry is analyzed quantitatively (Table A4).

Espresso-3D/2D as symmetric, minimal baselines is a sensible design choice to isolate the dataset's contribution from architecture effects, and the models themselves achieve competitive results (e.g., best LASO-unseen aIoU, strong zero-shot AGD20K transfer and synthetic-to-real results on Open X-Embodiment).

Writing is generally clear and the paper is well organized; implementation details in the appendix are sufficiently specific (models, GPUs, hyperparameters) to support reproduction of the training protocol.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is undermined by an empty 'Dataset link' section (Appendix A is a placeholder with no URL). For a paper whose central contribution is a dataset and benchmark, not releasing the data at submission time is a serious issue that alone could justify rejection if not remedied in the rebuttal.

There are signs of hasty preparation: figures and tables inconsistently name the model 'Espresso' vs. 'Gato' (Fig. 1 labels say 'Gato-3D'/'Gato-2D', Fig. 6 says 'Gato-3D (Ours)', Fig. A4 says 'Gato-2D (Ours)'), the claim 'modality-specific designs' contradicts the earlier statement of a unified architecture, and citation errors exist (e.g., 3D-AffordanceNet cited as [3] in Appendix C instead of [15]).

The pretraining gains on the established LASO benchmark are modest and inconsistent: OpenAD gains only 0.9%p aIoU unseen, PointRefer shows degradation on the seen split (-0.6 aIoU, -1.3 AUC, -2.9 SIM, worse MAE), and Espresso-3D's MAE degrades with pretraining in both seen and unseen splits. The paper reports these honestly, but they weaken the headline claim of broad transferable supervision, and error bars/significance tests are absent.

The test split is derived from the same VLM pipeline as the training data (queries by Gemma3, corrected by humans), so the benchmark's notion of correctness is anchored in the generative models' vocabulary and query distribution; this raises a potential circularity concern for evaluating open-vocabulary grounding in general, which is discussed only briefly.

The 2D split is a projection of the 3D heatmaps rather than independently validated 2D annotations; its domain gap with real images (acknowledged in Appendix C.2) means the 2D supervision may be of limited value for real-world applications beyond the background-augmentation trick.

Some self-defined dataset quality metrics (coverage, KL-diversity in Fig. 3d) are only compared against LASO and are not standard measures; the >450 classes / >350 affordances in Table 1 are themselves Gemma3 predictions, so the headline diversity numbers inherit pipeline noise.

Zero-shot 2D baselines in Table 4a are generic VLM-segmentation systems, not affordance-specific methods pretrained on comparable data, making the zero-shot comparison somewhat favorable to Espresso-2D; the supervised comparisons in Table 4b are more convincing.

Human validation covers only 5K of 750K pairs (0.67%), so the 84.8% success rate estimate has nontrivial uncertainty, and the training set's ~15% error rate is never mitigated (e.g., no confidence filtering of the train split is ablated).

strengths: Substantial and well-motivated dataset contribution: Affogato-750K (750K annotations over 150K 3D objects) clearly surpasses existing 3D/2D affordance datasets in scale and open-vocabulary coverage (Table 1), addressing a genuine data bottleneck in affordance grounding.

The fully automated annotation pipeline (Gemma3 -> Molmo -> MobileSAM with multi-view voting) is a sensible, well-described use of foundation models, and the paper transparently characterizes its failure modes (Fig. 4, App. C.1) rather than hiding them, including an 84.8% success rate from human validation.
The 5K human-verified test split, held out from training with no instance/view/query overlap, provides a reliable evaluation resource — a critical point for a model-generated dataset.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for a dataset paper: pretaining gains transfer across multiple architectures (OpenAD, PointRefer, Espresso) on the external LASO benchmark and AGD20K (Tables 2, 4), with held-out category filtering (Table 5) ruling out the obvious confound that gains come merely from covering benchmark classes.

Strong supporting analyses: pretaining-scale ablation (Table A3) substantiates the 'at scale' claim, the cross-domain asymmetry analysis (Table A4) is careful, and synthetic-to-real zero-shot transfer to Open X-Embodiment scenes probes domain gap. Backbone/ablation details (CoT prompting, mask-size selection, background augmentation, resolution) are included.

The Espresso models are appropriately framed as minimal baselines to isolate the dataset's contribution rather than as algorithmic novelty — an honest and correct scoping of the contribution type (Datasets/Benchmarks with supporting models).
Well-written and clearly organized; implementation details (Appendix B) are sufficient for reproduction of training.
weaknesses: Train-set annotation quality rests on automated predictions: only 5K of 750K pairs are human-verified (84.8% success), so roughly 15% of training labels may be flawed. The scale ablation mitigates this concern but does not directly quantify the effect of label noise on downstream performance (e.g., training on verified-only vs. full data).

No methodological novelty in the annotation pipeline itself: the approach is a straightforward orchestration of existing off-the-shelf models (Gemma3, Molmo, MobileSAM). The value is in execution and validation, which is legitimate for a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, but the pipeline's generality claim ('can be applied to other 3D datasets') is asserted rather than demonstrated on a second source.

Evaluation on the Affogato-750K test split (Table 3) is partially self-referential: GT labels come from the same pipeline (albeit human-verified/refined), and only methods retrained by the authors are compared, so results there are less diagnostic than the LASO/AGD20K transfer experiments.

Some inconsistencies and unexplained details: Table 1 reports '>450' classes and '>350' affordances only as Gemma3 frequency-filtered lower bounds; Section 1 says '150,104' 3D instances while the abstract says 150K; the definitions of coverage/diversity metrics (Table 3d/Fig. 3) are only sketched; PointRefer's seen-split aIoU drops with pretaining and the paper does not analyze why.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the 'Dataset link' section (App. A) is a placeholder with no URL or licensing/Objaverse redistribution terms; no code release is confirmed. For a dataset paper, public release of data, pipeline code, and the annotation UI is essential.

Societal impact discussion is absent beyond technical limitations; Objaverse assets are web-crawled, and potential biases of VLM-generated affordance concepts (e.g., culturally specific affordances) are not discussed.
Minor presentation issues: some figures are dense (Fig. 1), and the 2D rendering viewpoint selection heuristic (25 views, most-visible viewpoint) could bias the 2D split toward canonical poses.
